## A handshake protects no one

Leasing farmland still often happens on a handshake, between neighbours or long-time acquaintances. It works fine as long as the relationship stays cordial — and it becomes a problem the moment there's disagreement over upkeep, renewal, or the field's condition at the end of the lease. A written lease, even a simple one, avoids most of these situations.

## Duration and renewal terms

A farm lease should spell out its exact duration and the conditions for renewal — whether it renews automatically or not, what notice is required, and whether rent can be adjusted at each renewal. Without that clarity, a tenant may invest in improving a field with no guarantee of benefiting from it beyond a single season, which discourages any long-term upkeep.

## Maintaining the drainage network

Who's responsible for maintaining the drainage network — ditch cleaning, upkeep of existing subsurface drainage — over the course of the lease? This question, often overlooked, determines whether excess water that shows up during the lease gets addressed quickly or gets left alone simply because no one's sure whose job it is.

## Permitted uses and limits

The lease should specify which crops or uses are permitted, and whether changes in practice — a new rotation, added drainage, liming — require the landlord's prior agreement. This avoids misunderstandings about what falls under normal tenant management and what counts as a substantial change to the land.

## The land's condition at the start and end of the lease

Documenting the field's condition before the lease begins — and planning for the same documentation at the end — protects both parties. It prevents a disagreement over degradation or improvement from being settled years later based on nothing but memory. [This article](../etat-terrain-avant-bail/index.qmd) explains why this step benefits the landlord just as much as the tenant.

## A short contract, but a complete one

A farm lease doesn't need to be long to be solid. It just needs to cover these elements clearly, before signing, rather than relying on however well things happen to be going at the time.
